item.title: I Reconsidered My Stance on Obsidian After Building a Second Brain with 219,000 Files
item.description:
For over a year and a half, I've been building a digital twin: a knowledge base containing my life's data from the past decade, and an agent that uses this base. I started like everyone else, with Obsidian and Claude. My first conclusions came after uploading 219,353 files. For me, Obsidian is now just a viewer, not what I initially thought. The value of this data lies in three things: plain text files on disk, links and interconnections between them, and an agent that reads and writes them directly. This article explains how it's set up now and how many tokens have been spent. My goal was to create a digital twin – a system that thinks and responds like me, remembers everything I remember, and even what I've forgotten. This requires a properly functioning memory, not a vector database with 500-token blocks, but a structured one with history. I installed Obsidian, created a vault, and started dumping notes, documents, and stories – everything. I expected Obsidian to be the home of my memory, the graph to be a functional tool for finding forgotten information, not just a visual, and plugins to cover all my needs: linking notes, creating tables, and connecting to a neural network. I also expected seamless synchronization and for the agent to work with the base through it. Only the graph's aesthetics and the readability of notes met these expectations. Obsidian is not a knowledge base; for me, it's a viewer for a folder of text files. It's beautiful, with a graph and plugins. The agent doesn't need Obsidian at all. Claude Code reads and writes files directly, without bridge plugins or intermediaries. Synchronization also bypasses Obsidian's cloud. Syncthing works well; I have six machines, each with a full data copy. I'm keeping Obsidian for its graph visualization and note readability, but its role is far from what I imagined from reviews and descriptions. Perhaps my initial mistake was (and many make it) dumping everything into text files: chat logs, dumps. The vault grew rapidly, search worsened, and token usage increased due to sifting through irrelevant information. My current data storage and processing are structured in three layers. Layer 1: Facts. Raw data in SQLite databases (Telegram archive, browser history, counters). Questions of 'how much,' 'when,' and 'who' are resolved by database queries, costing zero tokens. Layer 2: Meaning. After selecting notes, I perform value-based search on my GPU, saving tokens. The agent queries it and receives the five closest notes for reading. Layer 3: Thoughts. The AI and I write summaries: decisions, rules, profiles, analyses. Raw information doesn't enter the vault. I use inexpensive tools first: database queries and file searches are free. Value-based search is cheap. The AI model is called last, only when its judgment is needed, and it receives pre-selected information. A mandatory rule: the agent must always retrieve context before starting work. For example, when writing an email, the agent reads the recipient's card, correspondence history, and past interactions. When starting a task, it checks if it's been done before. At the start of a session, it runs the query through search and works based on the input. Second rule: everything processed by the agent is saved. Each saved file undergoes four steps: the original is preserved, a note with a description and source is saved, the search is re-indexed, and links to neighboring notes are added. The note header includes title, date, type, source, machine, and tags. The 'machine' field is crucial as six machines and multiple people write to the vault, aiding in quick orientation. The most useful outcome is my voice profile. A script analyzed all 958,014 of my messages over ten years, collecting statistics on greetings, filler words, introductions, sales pitches, and reminders. Now, when the agent writes as me, it consults this profile to mimic my style. Messages after 2025 were counted separately as AI writing quality varied. Figures: 219,353 text files, 280 concepts (graph core), 5.9 GB Telegram archive (958,014 messages), 6 machines synced via Syncthing, value-based search on GPU. Challenges: Syncthing conflicts with multiple machines writing to one folder (mitigated by 'one file, one writer' rule and conflict monitoring script). Incorrect conclusions due to robots not finding information (now agent searches all locations before concluding absence). High cost of loading files per session (mitigated by measuring token cost of new rules and nightly compression). My logic: raw data to database, meaning to search, thoughts to text files. Violating this costs money. In the end: after 1.5 years, I have a vendor-independent memory: disk files, SQLite, open Syncthing. Obsidian and Claude can be replaced, but the files remain. The agent wakes up knowing the context: decisions made, promises given, yesterday's issues. Everything described is on my GitHub. Feel free to ask questions; I'm happy to share my 1.5 years of setup and reconfiguration.

item.title: AI Agents: What They Are, How They Work, and How Our Assistant's Agent Mode is Structured
item.description:
The AI landscape has recently undergone a significant paradigm shift. Previously, we discussed intelligent assistants automating narrow scenarios like documentation Q&A or support bots. Now, technology has advanced to a point where complex human actions can be automated using various planning tools, multi-step task execution, and more – all of which are now termed AI agents. Many companies are releasing their own solutions, and open-source options are also available. While there's a lot of hype around the topic, with many half-working prototypes, there are also scenarios where agents prove genuinely useful and are already helping solve business problems. Read more

item.title: AI Agent to the Rescue: How We Automated Over 70% of Analyst Routine and Increased Team Efficiency
item.description:
Hi! My name is Dmitry Gavrilov, and I'm the head of the analytics competence center at MWS. My team is integrating AI skills into the work of data analysts. We looked at a typical workday and realized that routine consumes up to 75% of an analyst's time. Can this be delegated to an AI agent without loss of quality? We tested this hypothesis on real tasks and got concrete results – I'm sharing them in this article. Read on

item.title: Choosing a UI Tool for Rapid Prototyping in AI Products: Open WebUI
item.description:
When developing an AI product, we faced an unexpected challenge. Choosing an LLM turned out to be easier than choosing an interface for it. Ready-made AI chats are well-suited for dialogue with a single model, but they start to limit the product when it includes multiple agents, complex scenarios, and intermediate work stages. In this article, we will describe the essence of the task, the requirements, and analyze Open WebUI. Read more

item.title: How to interact with AI and not lose data?
item.description:
Wake me up at night and ask 'what not to do with AI', and I'll answer 'upload confidential data'. This rule should be ingrained in us like the multiplication table. It should be, but it's not a fact that it works in 100% of cases, especially if you play with AI not for work, but for personal purposes. Well, what could happen if I just ask the model to translate a piece of text from Elvish Sindarin into ordinary human language? If you are as anxious a paranoid as I am, then inside for you are a few simple settings for AI chats to sleep soundly. Yes, this is not an absolute guarantee that nothing will leak anywhere and the model will not learn anything from you, but, as they say, God protects those who protect themselves. And I will also show the full cycle of connecting your key to an AI client (footnote: an application where you can connect several AI models from different providers at once and work with them in one interface) using ChatBox as an example. It will be interesting for those who are just starting their acquaintance with the world of AI and want to try to safely integrate it into their processes. Read more

item.title: Four Copies of the Project and One Lab Monster. How to Teach an AI Agent to Write Code According to Design System Rules
item.description:
The screen looked almost alive. The model assembled a page with cards, statuses, and badges in minutes. It seemed I could put my feet up and finish my coffee. But then the code reached review. Beneath the neat interface were styled.div, HEX colors, and props that never existed in our design system. The result was that very lab monster, wheezing but unable to live in the project. So, I conducted an experiment with one frontend task, one model, and four identical copies of the project. In the first case, I left the agent without hints; in the second, I gave it a skill with project rules; in the third, I connected MCP with design system documentation; and in the fourth, I combined everything. I wanted to find out which combination would turn code generation into an elixir of speed, and which would spawn another monster unable to survive an encounter with typecheck and build. Read on.

item.title: Skynet or Scamnet? How Corporations Sold Us a Fantasy of "Artificial Intelligence" for Billions
item.description:
Two millennials who sold the world $850 billion worth of neural networks disguised as "AI" are looking at you from the cover of Time magazine. They try to look friendly, but honestly, it's the uncanny valley effect. The caption "TRUST US" in huge letters looks like a mockery, but no, they are serious. In the article under the cover, Altman and Brockman AGAIN promise to create "real AI" (what was there before?) - this time by the end of 2026. Do we believe them? In this article, I will explain why the loud news that "AI agents" "hacked" someone on their own initiative is simply the biggest PR campaign in history - and how it is supposed to cover up the biggest financial pyramid in history, based on a deliberately false interpretation of the concept of "artificial intelligence." And also under the cut - why Richard Dawkins, who recognized the presence of consciousness in "AI," did not go mad in his old age, but fell into the trap of his own scientism (and the influence of Daniel Dennett). Make yourselves comfortable. Read more

item.title: "Anime Factory" Opened: Releasing the Code for a Pipeline That Cuts Episodes into Shorts Itself
item.description:
Recently, I've written three articles about a system that turns long videos into vertical clips: a general overview of the "anime factory", a breakdown of a virtual camera with face tracking, and a story about why the "transcript + LLM" combination almost always yields garbage. The comment that was repeated under all three was the same: "show the code." Here it is. → github.com/ialakey/shorts-factory This is a showcase branch of a large private project: an MVP that retains the full path "take a long video → get a ready-made vertical clip", with everything else cut out. Below is what's inside, how the code relates to the three previous articles, and what had to be thrown out. Take a look behind the scenes.

item.title: One, the Best, or All Together? Seven Bugs, Four Fixers, and Seven Assemblers
item.description:
One broken bash script. Seven real bugs—from cosmetic (outdated filenames in comments) to fatal: a summary table that always shows zeros, no matter what actually happens. Four models fix this script blindly, independently, unaware of what the other three are doing. Then, seven more models receive all four finished fixes as input and one task: assemble the best from them. Spoiler alert—just enough to not spoil the intrigue: at the start, the models diverge much more than one might expect. No single model found everything. And their blind spots don't overlap. Therefore, the experiment is worth conducting rather than just discussing theoretically. Read more

Original Russian article on Habr

item.title: Can AI Port an App to Aurora OS? An Experiment with Mattermost and RuStore Publication
item.description:
Hello, this is the Aurora OS team. We have a problem that is not usually discussed in vendor blogs, but without it, this whole story makes no sense. We regularly hear the same thing about Aurora: the platform is good, but there are few apps, and porting ready-made Android apps to it is difficult and expensive. A pet project is fine. A corporate application is also fine: we have many of them, they just live within closed environments, and you don't see them. But a mass-market application that needs an audience of millions to exist seems doomed: no one will rewrite a million lines of legacy code for a new platform. The conversation usually boils down to the same phrase: everything we have is native. Kotlin, Swift, years of accumulated code, and rewriting it is long and expensive. Not everyone has cross-platform. For those who do, we've long had an answer: Flutter for Aurora is officially supported, Compose Multiplatform is too, and such teams migrate without drama. But for everyone else, until recently, we could only offer sympathy. Now, in the era of AI, a tool more powerful than any SDK has emerged, and it would be strange not to try it. Therefore, we took someone else's large application, invited an external expert whom we do not control in any way, and agreed to publish the result regardless of how it turns out. Read more

item.title: The "Archangel" Architecture: How to Deploy an On-Premise Multi-Agent AI System in an Isolated Environment
item.description:
Recently, businesses have been increasingly looking towards Agentic AI – systems where neural networks don't just respond to prompts in a chat but act as autonomous digital employees. When it comes to large enterprises, compliance, and working with sensitive data (e.g., legal or financial documents), cloud APIs from OpenAI or Anthropic immediately become a showstopper. Security demands complete isolation. In this article, I will technically break down how we designed and implemented the "Archangel" On-Premise multi-agent AI platform, capable of operating without external internet access. 1. Delivery and Infrastructure Layer: Full On-Premise in Kubernetes For large customers, it is critically important that software is deployed within their own isolated perimeter (On-Premise) and managed using tools familiar to their Ops teams. We abandoned complex proprietary installers in favor of containerization. We deliver the "Archangel" platform as isolated Helm charts for the customer's Kubernetes cluster. This ensures predictable deployment and easy scaling under load. Isolation is provided not by the packaging itself, but by network policies and the absence of an external route – more on this below. How it works at the infrastructure level: - Air-gapped environment. All platform's base Docker images and local LLM weights (e.g., Llama or Mistral families, adapted for our tasks) are mirrored to the customer's internal private registry – Harbor or Nexus. - State and Storage. Within the Helm charts, StatefulSets are described for databases and message brokers, which can use either internal K8s storage (via CSI) or connect to existing PostgreSQL or Redis clusters within the customer's environment. Read more

item.title: How We Taught ML to Predict Pump Failure 60 Days in Advance and Discovered We Were Always Fixing the Wrong Thing (Part 1)
item.description:
A pump at an oil refinery broke down every three months. Repair crews replaced bearings, but the problem persisted. We proposed not just monitoring vibration, but finding the hidden cause in the data. The result exceeded expectations: 60 days of advance warning and an unexpected culprit. We explain how it happened and why the model is only 20% of the success. Learn why they were fixing the wrong thing.
